title: Why Braille Made Night Writing Simple
topic: Why Louis Braille turned army night writing into raised dots

lines: A soldier punches twelve tiny dots into paper in the dead of night.
His comrades laugh, saying the code is useless and too slow.
Blind teen Louis Braille watches the demo at his school.
He grabs the same slate and stylus.
He spends months feeling each pattern.
Then he halves the grid to three high and two wide.
You see, it’s like turning a bulky novel into a pocket‑size cheat sheet you can feel with one fingertip.
Barbier’s army night‑writing used twelve raised points to spell sounds, but soldiers could not master it.
Braille cut the pattern in half, using only six dots to stand for letters, numbers and punctuation.
Six dots sit comfortably under a single finger.
A reader can feel a whole character in one quick touch.
Writers can punch the dots faster than they could trace letters.
Ironically, the system meant for soldiers became the world’s universal language for the blind.

claims.claim: Charles Barbier, a retired artillery captain, invented night writing with twelve raised dots for soldiers to communicate in the dark.
Soldiers found Barbier’s twelve‑dot code too hard and it was never accepted.
Louis Braille reduced the code to six dots (three high, two wide) and simplified it to represent letters rather than sounds.
The six‑dot cell fits in a fingertip, allowing reading with a single touch.
